jokes.text: I was in the middle of bidding on a bag of bras on eBay.
jokes.setup: Jack urgently summons Liz, implying something serious.
jokes.punchline: Liz reveals she was doing something pathetically mundane — bidding on a bulk bag of bras on eBay.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'a bag of bras' (not just bras, but a bag of them, plural) makes this perfectly calibrated Liz Lemon character comedy. It's not just self-deprecating — it's a portrait of her chaotic, slightly sad domestic life delivered in total deadpan. High character integration because only Liz would both do this and say it out loud to her boss.

jokes.text: It's not, Hon. I saw that in a movie once, but in the movie, the guy was dead.
jokes.setup: Liz asks if Hank Hooper wanting to meet is a good thing. Jack says 'It's not, Hon' — a phrase Liz notes she heard in a movie.
jokes.punchline: Jack confirms he also got it from a movie — one where the character receiving that phrase was dead.
jokes.explanation: Tight two-step structure: Liz catches the movie reference, Jack confirms it while casually escalating the horror — the guy in the movie was dead. Jack's utter calm delivery of a death sentence is quintessential Donaghy. Well-constructed and economical.

jokes.text: Nope. That was me. What can I say. I smell like leather.
jokes.setup: Jack asks how long Hank has been in the room. Hank says he was sitting in the chair a minute ago. Jack says that was him.
jokes.punchline: Hank doubles down — it was him, not Jack — and explains he smells like leather as if that's the clarifying detail.
jokes.explanation: Hank Hooper is immediately established as a cheerfully absurd character. The leather detail is a non-sequitur that functions as instant character building — folksy, odd, confident. Good economy.

jokes.text: Well, I'll be Bake McBrided. I know a Philly gal when I hug one.
jokes.setup: Hank meets Liz and immediately hugs her.
jokes.punchline: 'I'll be Bake McBrided' — a folksy Philly-specific corruption of 'I'll be damned,' using the name of a Philadelphia figure, delivered with total sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Specific and confident absurdism. 'Bake McBride' is a real Phillies outfielder — it's a hyper-specific cultural reference used to build a folksy exclamation that feels authentic to the character's regional identity. The hug detail adds a physical comedy layer.

jokes.text: Without Tracy, your show is like my cholesterol. The numbers are killing me.
jokes.setup: Hank is about to say something bad about TGS's ratings.
jokes.punchline: He compares the show's numbers to his cholesterol — which he reveals is also bad (killing him) — a folksy analogy that doubles as a health confession.
jokes.explanation: The folksy analogy that also reveals personal medical information is perfectly Hank Hooper. He's built as an earnest, plain-spoken, slightly unhealthy Philly guy. The joke works because the analogy is structurally sound (both the show and his health are in bad shape) while being absurdly personal.

jokes.text: The show is number 1 in its time slot among men 18 to 49 months left in prison.
jokes.setup: Liz pitches the show's ratings success — 'number 1 in its time slot among men 18 to 49...'
jokes.punchline: '...months left in prison' — the demographic isn't age-based, it's prison-sentence-based.
jokes.explanation: One of the sharpest jokes in the episode. The setup perfectly mimics the standard Nielsen demographic boilerplate ('men 18 to 49') then lands a grammatical trap — '49 months left in prison' retrofits 'to 49' as a duration rather than an age. It's rapid, unexpected, devastating about the show's actual audience quality, and beautifully economical. Highly quotable and a textbook 30 Rock misdirection joke. Justifiably scores near the top.

jokes.text: I thought this company was a family, but I guess it's that Austrian family and I am the girl in the basement and you are the dad who has been brutally...
jokes.setup: Liz is trying to emotionally appeal to Hank by invoking the idea of 'family.'
jokes.punchline: She pivots to referencing the Fritzl case — the infamous Austrian basement captivity — before Jack cuts her off.
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels: Liz's rhetorical incompetence (her 'family' defense veers into something horrifying), the show's willingness to go dark, and the perfectly timed Jack cut-off before she fully articulates the atrocity. The incompleteness is funnier than the completion would be. Strong Liz character integration — she's trying to be persuasive and failing catastrophically.

jokes.text: All right. You get one more shot. Just like the Army doctor said to me after my weekend in Okinawa!
jokes.setup: Hank grants TGS one more shot.
jokes.punchline: He cheerfully recalls an Army doctor giving him the same phrase after some unspecified debauchery in Okinawa.
jokes.explanation: Hank Hooper's folksy cheerfulness applied to something clearly dark and embarrassing (army doctor, Okinawa, 'one more shot' in a medical context) is a reliable character comedy beat. The implication is left delightfully vague. Good character integration for this recurring 'folksy dark past' trait.

jokes.text: They're mean. Jack Welch once smacked a pretzel out of my hand at the Super Bowl.
jokes.setup: Hank comments on Kabletown vs. GE, saying it's no wonder Jack is at Kabletown instead of running GE.
jokes.punchline: His evidence that GE is 'mean': Jack Welch personally smacked a pretzel out of his hand at the Super Bowl.
jokes.explanation: The specificity is everything — not just 'GE is mean,' but Jack Welch, specifically, at the Super Bowl, specifically knocking a pretzel. It's a vivid, petty grievance that humanizes both Hank and the absurdity of corporate power. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Is Tracy back? I'd hate to think I just lied to Hank. Jeez, I'll get it done. You know I'll do whatever it takes, Lemon style.
jokes.setup: Jack realizes Liz may have fabricated Tracy's return. Liz admits uncertainty but commits to fixing it.
jokes.punchline: 'Lemon style' — invoking her own name as a brand of competence, which given all evidence is deeply ironic.
jokes.explanation: Functional self-awareness joke from Liz. 'Lemon style' works as ironic self-branding but isn't particularly sharp. The setup is good (she lied to the boss), but the punchline doesn't fully capitalize on it.

jokes.text: Everybody dance now! [Tracy is shown doing the C+C Music Factory dance in the middle of a chaotic scene]
jokes.setup: Liz commits to handling the Tracy situation. Cut to Tracy.
jokes.punchline: Tracy is inexplicably shouting 'Everybody dance now!' — an absurdist non-sequitur establishing his current unhinged state.
jokes.explanation: Pure Tracy absurdism. The juxtaposition between Liz's serious problem-solving and Tracy's random C+C Music Factory outburst is a classic 30 Rock whiplash cut. Character-specific and economical.

jokes.text: But you're going to get me another sandwich, or I'm going to cut your face up so bad, you'll have a chin. I will waste you!
jokes.setup: Tracy is described as still being 'crazy' and in character as D'Jeffrey.
jokes.punchline: The threat escalates absurdly — 'cut your face up so bad, you'll have a chin' is a uniquely Tracy-logic insult (having a chin is the bad outcome).
jokes.explanation: The inversion — 'you'll have a chin' as the threatening consequence — is genuinely inventive. It's Tracy-brand absurdist threat-making where the logic is broken but internally consistent. 'I will waste you' as a coda is perfectly timed. High quotability and strong character integration.

jokes.text: You'll have to go through this old bastard first! And I don't really think it's fair for me to be on a jury because I'm a hologram.
jokes.setup: Someone defends against Tracy's threat.
jokes.punchline: The defender pivots mid-sentence to worrying about jury duty because he's a hologram — a completely left-field non-sequitur.
jokes.explanation: Pure 30 Rock absurdism — the hologram jury duty concern is a perfect throwaway that deepens the sense of chaos around Tracy. The non-sequitur structure is clean: heroic setup, bizarre pivot.

jokes.text: He told me he feels like a Bartram's Scrub-Hairstreak trying to crawl back into its silky cocoon which is a butterfly metaphor, by the way, and not, as I first thought, a list of African-American hair products.
jokes.setup: Liz explains Tracy's emotional state using his own metaphor.
jokes.punchline: She clarifies it's a butterfly metaphor — 'not, as I first thought, a list of African-American hair products.'
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional 30 Rock writing. The joke operates on multiple levels: the absurd specificity of the butterfly name ('Bartram's Scrub-Hairstreak'), Liz's earnest clarification of the metaphor, and the revelation that she genuinely thought it was a hair product list — which is both racially self-aware comedy and a perfect portrait of Liz's confused well-meaning. The structure is impeccable: setup the confusion, clarify, reveal the initial misreading. One of the episode's best jokes.

jokes.text: Well, you just need to turn the beautiful butterfly back into a drunk, incompetent caterpillar.
jokes.setup: Liz has used the butterfly metaphor. Jack responds with a solution.
jokes.punchline: The goal is to reverse Tracy's growth — back to 'drunk, incompetent caterpillar' — which Jack delivers with complete executive seriousness.
jokes.explanation: A perfect callback payoff. Jack takes Liz's butterfly metaphor and weaponizes it — the plan is to reverse the metamorphosis, which inverts all standard inspirational rhetoric. 'Drunk, incompetent caterpillar' as a goal is a devastating encapsulation of what TGS needs and what the show is about. Jack's executive confidence makes the absurdity land harder. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Jesus was black! [Tracy shouts this on a morning show when asked about Mar-A-Lago]
jokes.setup: A morning show host is making pleasant small talk with Tracy about Mar-A-Lago, implying Tracy has been 'prepped' to behave.
jokes.punchline: Tracy immediately destroys the warm atmosphere with a non-sequitur declaration.
jokes.explanation: Three words that blow up the entire polite interview setup. Economy is near-perfect. The contrast between the genteel Mar-A-Lago conversation and this outburst is the joke. Strong Tracy character integration — this is exactly what he'd do.

jokes.text: Really? Is it from that pie place?
jokes.setup: Jack says he's tired of 'going to bat' for Liz and has 'a very full plate.'
jokes.punchline: Liz's brain immediately converts 'full plate' to a literal plate of pie — she asks if it's from a specific pie place.
jokes.explanation: Distilled Liz Lemon character comedy — her food obsession literally interrupts her ability to process metaphors. The follow-up 'There is no pie. Okay.' exchange makes it even better. Perfect character integration; this is definitionally Liz.

jokes.text: There is no pie. Okay.
jokes.setup: Liz has asked about pie. Jack has to clarify.
jokes.punchline: Jack's flat 'There is no pie' — said as if correcting a child — and Liz's defeated 'Okay' is the payoff.
jokes.explanation: The callback payoff to the pie joke. Four words total, two beats, perfect. Liz's 'Okay' communicates genuine sadness. The economy is exceptional — it's a complete mini-scene in two lines.

jokes.text: Who wears a swimsuit to Denny's? That's her! That's Pam! The overly confident morbidly obese woman.
jokes.setup: The TGS crew is filming their recurring 'Pam' sketch for the 100th episode.
jokes.punchline: The description of 'Pam' — 'the overly confident morbidly obese woman' who wears a swimsuit to Denny's — as a celebrated recurring character.
jokes.explanation: The joke is meta — TGS's most beloved recurring sketch is a one-note caricature, and the specificity of 'Denny's' and 'overly confident' sells it. It's commentary on what passes for hit television comedy.

jokes.text: In 100 shows, we've done 'Pam' 107 times.
jokes.setup: Celebration of the 100th episode.
jokes.punchline: 107 times in 100 shows — they've done it more than once per episode, which is either laziness or desperation (both funnier).
jokes.explanation: The math joke — 107 times in 100 episodes — is the punchline, and it lands hard because it quantifies the creative bankruptcy of TGS while played as a proud accomplishment. Sharp structural economy.

jokes.text: That wasn't me. There used to be another guy. I don't think so.
jokes.setup: Jenna claims 'we've had an amazing 5 years.' Danny points out he wasn't there from the start.
jokes.punchline: Jenna flatly denies the existence of any prior cast member — 'I don't think so' — with complete confidence.
jokes.explanation: Jenna's narcissism erases inconvenient facts — she simply refuses to acknowledge anyone else existed. The dismissive 'I don't think so' is perfectly Jenna and economically delivered.

jokes.text: I will choke you to death with your boyfriend's wig!
jokes.setup: Jenna is being wished happy 100th show.
jokes.punchline: She erupts into a threat involving her co-star's boyfriend's wig — a hyper-specific threat that implies entire unseen backstory.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'your boyfriend's wig' does a lot of work — there's an entire implied drama in that phrase. Jenna's explosive violence delivered in a celebratory context is a strong character beat.

jokes.text: Give me back my man, bitch!
jokes.setup: Jenna's violent outburst continues.
jokes.punchline: The threat clarifies — there's a love triangle involving the boyfriend whose wig was mentioned.
jokes.explanation: Extends the Jenna violence bit but adds less than the previous line. The escalation is slight. Functional but not exceptional on its own.

jokes.text: Can you reminisce about something that's happened since I've been here, 'cause I couldn't see any of that.
jokes.setup: Jenna and the others are reminiscing about the early show before Danny joined.
jokes.punchline: Danny points out he literally can't participate in the nostalgia because he wasn't there yet.
jokes.explanation: A meta joke about the show's own history and cast turnover. Competent but not particularly elevated.

jokes.text: Terrific show, Ma'am. If I know anything about television, The Girlie Show is a hit! Oh, please. If this turkey goes 100 episodes, I'll have your baby.
jokes.setup: A flashback to after the very first episode of TGS.
jokes.punchline: Young Jenna's dismissive 'If this turkey goes 100 episodes, I'll have your baby' — which is now the premise of the current episode.
jokes.explanation: This flashback joke works as both a setup for the episode's Jenna subplot AND a standalone ironic punchline. The casual flippancy of Jenna's promise — essentially a bet she was certain she'd never have to honor — is perfectly in character. The irony of the show reaching 100 episodes despite her confidence it would fail is structurally elegant.

jokes.text: I said that? I was so young. Wait, I saw that. How? Am I dead?
jokes.setup: Jenna watches the flashback of herself.
jokes.punchline: Jenna's reaction is three separate comedic beats: denial of memory, denial of aging, then existential confusion about how she could see a flashback at all.
jokes.explanation: The meta-confusion ('Am I dead?') acknowledges the absurdity of sitcom flashbacks from within the fiction. Jenna's vanity ('I was so young') and her logical breakdown about seeing herself are all strong character beats stacked efficiently.

jokes.text: Well, it's been 100 episodes, I better lay you across my grandmother's lap in the mating shed.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is responding to Jenna's old promise to have his baby.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's response involves a 'mating shed' and his grandmother's lap — suggesting a horrifying rural reproductive tradition.
jokes.explanation: Kenneth's 'mating shed' is one of those perfectly 30 Rock-specific absurdist details that deepens the character's mythology while being simultaneously horrifying and hilarious. The grandmother's lap adds a layer that makes it worse in the best possible way. Maximum Kenneth Parcell character specificity.

jokes.text: I wish. Albinos get to be watchers in the mating shed.
jokes.setup: Someone calls Kenneth an 'albino goon' in exasperation.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth corrects the record — he's not an albino, and importantly, albinos have a specific privileged role in the mating shed hierarchy.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the mating shed mythology is exceptional. By adding a social hierarchy within the shed — albinos as 'watchers,' a distinct role — the joke deepens an already absurd world. Kenneth's wistful 'I wish' implies he genuinely envies albino shed-watchers. This is peak Kenneth Parcell world-building comedy. The economy is excellent and the callback structure is tight.

jokes.text: A picture of you in US Weekly next to Natalie Portman in the same maternity outfit, 'Who wore it best?' I did. I wore it best.
jokes.setup: Liz is hypothetically imagining Jenna as a pregnant celebrity.
jokes.punchline: Without missing a beat, Jenna self-awards herself the 'who wore it best' competition.
jokes.explanation: Jenna's unearned confidence and narcissism expressed through the 'I wore it best' self-assessment is sharp. Natalie Portman as the comparator is a good specific choice. The rhythm — hypothetical scenario, Jenna's flat self-assertion — is clean.

jokes.text: So, we're counting on Tracy? Forget it!
jokes.setup: Liz announces the show's survival depends on Tracy returning.
jokes.punchline: Frank immediately gives up — his reaction acknowledging the impossibility of relying on Tracy.
jokes.explanation: A quick, economical reaction beat. Frank's immediate despair is character-consistent and gets a small laugh but is a fairly basic gag.

jokes.text: [Flashback montage of bad times: 'Riding straight to hell!' / 'Here come the roofies.' / 'Where's my mac and cheese?'
jokes.setup: Liz is giving a pep talk, saying they've 'been through bad times before.'
jokes.punchline: The 'bad times' flashbacks are a rapid-fire series of chaotic quotes, each worse than the last, culminating in 'Where's my mac and cheese?' as somehow equally catastrophic.
jokes.explanation: The montage structure — 'here come the roofies' as a low point, then 'where's my mac and cheese?' as the final bad memory — works through accumulation and the absurdity of the last item deflating the drama. Standard 30 Rock montage comedy executed well.

jokes.text: [Flashback to good times: 'Who wants... my puddings!'
jokes.setup: After bad times, Liz pivots to good times.
jokes.punchline: The 'good time' is someone enthusiastically offering puddings — the mundane specificity of 'my puddings' as a peak moment.
jokes.explanation: The contrast with the 'bad times' montage is the joke — the 'good time' is just someone offering puddings. Works through deflation and the plural 'puddings' carrying an inexplicable enthusiasm.

jokes.text: Tonight, 'TGS' will not be the worst thing on television. It'll be John Stossel!
jokes.setup: Liz's pep talk builds toward an inspirational climax.
jokes.punchline: The motivational goal: not to be the worst, just to be better than John Stossel.
jokes.explanation: Structurally brilliant subversion of the inspirational speech. Liz's goal isn't excellence — it's merely to not be the absolute worst, and she names a specific person as the floor. The specificity of John Stossel (a real journalist/personality with a reputation for controversy) makes it land harder than a generic name would. The crowd cheer — 'Yeah! Let's do it!' — in response to this non-ambition is the icing.

jokes.text: Gas leak, huh? Great. Damn it! Why now, on my last day before retirement? Here, let me show you guys something. That's my girl. We're getting married when I get out of here. Why am I showing you guys this? It's going to jinx everything. Plus, you're a couple of pervs.
jokes.setup: A maintenance worker is responding to a gas leak emergency on his last day before retirement.
jokes.punchline: He immediately breaks the 'last day before retirement' jinx by showing his girlfriend's photo, then catches himself — calling the responders pervs for... looking at a photo he showed them.
jokes.explanation: A meta-joke about the 'last day before retirement' trope in action-movie/cop shows. The character is actively living the cliché while aware enough to know it will jinx him — then compounds it by calling responders pervs for his own overshare. The self-awareness and self-destruction are perfectly timed.

jokes.text: Who's up there? 'TGS'? Isn't that show already half-dead?
jokes.setup: Workers discover the gas leak is going into the TGS floor.
jokes.punchline: One worker's reaction is a meta-commentary on TGS's quality/state.
jokes.explanation: Competent meta-joke about TGS's precarious status, but the character is a stranger and the joke lacks specificity. Functional.

jokes.text: Who wants to kiss? Let's say we get some fresh air.
jokes.setup: The gas leak begins affecting people on the TGS floor.
jokes.punchline: A character randomly propositions everyone for kisses, then suggests fresh air as a redirect.
jokes.explanation: An establishing joke for the gas-as-truth-serum/hallucination premise. Functional but not particularly inventive on its own.

jokes.text: Do you know what I find fascinating? Mystery novels written by janitors?
jokes.setup: Liz interrupts Jack to tell him about the gas leak. He deflects with a rhetorical question.
jokes.punchline: His hypothetical fascination — 'mystery novels written by janitors' — is a specific, dismissive non-answer that reveals his worldview.
jokes.explanation: Jack's rhetorical deflection with a randomly specific thing is well-executed. 'Mystery novels written by janitors' is the kind of absurdly specific dismissal that only Jack would deploy. Character-specific and economical.

jokes.text: See? I got a new hair. It's white and it hurts, but...
jokes.setup: Jack is insisting he's busy with many other things besides TGS.
jokes.punchline: His proof of being busy/vital: a single new white hair — which hurts.
jokes.explanation: Jack holding up a single new hair as evidence of his busy, vital existence while noting it 'hurts' is a good small character beat — his vanity and his insecurity about his stagnation compressed into one detail. The interruption before he finishes adds to it.

jokes.text: Other possible side-effects include hallucinations, revelation of secrets, telling of truths, flashbacks, headaches, nostalgia.
jokes.setup: The maintenance team is explaining the gas leak's medical effects.
jokes.punchline: The side effects perfectly describe what will happen in the episode — the gas is literally causing the episode's plot devices (flashbacks, nostalgia, truth-telling) to be announced as 'side effects.'
jokes.explanation: A clever meta-structural joke — the gas's side effects are a literal description of all the episode's narrative devices. The show is explaining its own premise while making a medical announcement. 'Nostalgia' as a side effect at the end is perfect, and 'headaches' grounds it. Strong meta-writing.

jokes.text: Can you believe this is happening to me on my last day of work? My last day. I don't know if there was a party planned...
jokes.setup: The retirement subplot continues — he keeps invoking 'my last day.'
jokes.punchline: He adds anxiety about whether a party was planned — this detail makes his 'last day' jinx feel increasingly sad and real.
jokes.explanation: Keeps the running gag alive with a small escalation (the party detail), but it's getting diminishing returns at this point. Competent continuation.

jokes.text: I refuse to have long, gas-induced conversations with any of you people.
jokes.setup: Jack is told about the gas and its side effects.
jokes.punchline: Jack preemptively refuses to have the very conversations the episode is structured around — a meta-awareness of the premise.
jokes.explanation: Jack resisting the episode's own premise is a strong meta joke. His refusal is perfectly in character — he despises emotional vulnerability — and the specificity of 'gas-induced' as the adjective he objects to is excellent. He's acknowledging the conceit while rejecting it, which is peak Jack Donaghy. Justifies 8+ for character integration and meta-structural wit.

jokes.text: Thank you. Pete. Thank you, Pete. [Jack accepts congratulations from Pete with regal, meaningless acknowledgment]
jokes.setup: Pete is thanking Jack for the 100th episode.
jokes.punchline: Jack's response — a slow, monarchical acknowledgment of Pete by name, twice — suggests he's already slightly gas-affected or simply always this imperious.
jokes.explanation: A small beat that works primarily as performance — Jack's regal repetition of 'Pete' is a character texture joke, implying either early gas effects or his baseline imperious nature. Modest but functional.

jokes.text: I can't believe it's been 100 shows. More like 100 little strokes.
jokes.setup: The 100th episode milestone is being acknowledged.
jokes.punchline: Pete reframes the achievement as '100 little strokes' — the show has been killing him, medically.
jokes.explanation: Pete's deeply depressed relationship to TGS is perfectly expressed in this line. 'More like 100 little strokes' is a great dark reframe of the milestone — the economy is excellent, and it's very specifically Pete's worldview. The medical specificity (strokes, not 'headaches' or 'nightmares') is a well-chosen detail.

jokes.text: I had a boyfriend, Denis. I mean, sure, he was an idiot, but he made great chili, and he didn't care if I watched TV during sex.
jokes.setup: Gas-affected Liz is nostalgically revisiting her pre-Jack life — specifically, her old boyfriend Denis.
jokes.punchline: Her defense of Denis bottoms out at 'didn't care if I watched TV during sex' — a damning and hilarious character detail.
jokes.explanation: The cumulative nature of this joke — the faint praise ('sure, he was an idiot, but') building to a very specific, very Liz form of romantic compatibility — is excellent. Watching TV during sex as Liz's romantic ideal is a perfectly chosen detail that's both funny in itself and revealing of her character. High character integration.

jokes.text: The gas is not affecting me yet, so I can lead you to safety. Just follow these... troll penises!
jokes.setup: Liz confidently declares she's unaffected by the gas and tries to lead people to safety.
jokes.punchline: Mid-sentence, the gas hits — 'troll penises' replaces whatever direction she was about to give.
jokes.explanation: The structure is near-perfect: Liz's confident self-assessment ('not affecting me yet') immediately collapsed by the gas hitting mid-sentence, landing on 'troll penises' as the hallucination. The timing, the specificity of the phrase, and Liz's horrified 'Oh God, what have I done?' coda all contribute. This is among the episode's best jokes.

jokes.text: Why don't you shut your mouth, back that ass up, and make me a sandwich!
jokes.setup: Tracy appears on a morning talk show as an Oscar-winning celebrity who is supposed to be doing a charming interview.
jokes.punchline: He immediately opens with an aggressive, misogynistic command — in character as D'Jeffrey but clearly also as himself.
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition with the gentle morning show setting is the joke. Tracy's in-character behavior being indistinguishable from his out-of-character behavior is a recurring theme. The hosts' awed reaction ('He's awesome!') deepens the irony.

jokes.text: He's awesome! You are still in character as the verbally abusive D'Jeffrey.
jokes.setup: Tracy verbally abuses the morning show hosts.
jokes.punchline: The hosts interpret it as committed method acting and praise him for it.
jokes.explanation: The hosts' oblivious adulation in the face of Tracy's abuse is a sharp satire of celebrity worship and morning show sycophancy. 'He's awesome!' as a response to 'shut your mouth, back that ass up' is the joke.

jokes.text: I lied to all you ugly white ladies. I didn't go to Africa. I was hiding in a warehouse in Queens watching vintage pornography. I love your honesty.
jokes.setup: The host tries to discuss Tracy's 'inspiring' post-Oscar trip to Africa.
jokes.punchline: Tracy reveals he lied — he was in Queens watching vintage pornography. The host's response: 'I love your honesty.'
jokes.explanation: Multi-layered: Tracy's revelation is funny, but the host calling it 'honesty' to celebrate rather than recoil is the sharper joke — it satirizes how celebrity confessionals are rewarded no matter the content. 'Ugly white ladies' as his opening address and 'vintage pornography' as the specific activity are both well-chosen details.

jokes.text: No, it's un-brave! You should hate me! I can't. You fly free. I'm a bird in a cage.
jokes.setup: Tracy tries to get the hosts to hate him. The host calls his behavior 'brave.'
jokes.punchline: Tracy's exasperated 'No, it's un-brave! You should hate me!' vs. the host's ethereal 'You fly free. I'm a bird in a cage.'
jokes.explanation: The escalating failure of Tracy's attempt to be hated — every outburst inspiring more admiration — is a strong running comic premise. The host's 'You fly free. I'm a bird in a cage' is an absurdly poetic non-response that deepens the satire.

jokes.text: Hey, you got to say around. We've got our no-cook cooking hair make-unders. What does that even mean? It's new haircuts, but you can make salads with them.
jokes.setup: The host tries to keep Tracy for a segment.
jokes.punchline: 'No-cook cooking hair make-unders' — a portmanteau segment name that combines cooking, hair, and make-unders. 'It's new haircuts, but you can make salads with them.'
jokes.explanation: This is a sharp satire of the meaningless morning show segment — combining too many buzzwords into an incomprehensible product. The explanation ('haircuts but you can make salads with them') doesn't clarify anything, which is the point. Good absurdist economy.

jokes.text: Frank, what is this? 'Broken eyboard alk show'? I write what I know. Also, I broke my keyboard.
jokes.setup: Liz is looking at Frank's sketch ideas outside, where they've evacuated.
jokes.punchline: Frank's sketch is 'Broken keyboard talk show' — but missing the letters his keyboard is missing — and he defends it with 'I write what I know' before adding the mundane practical explanation.
jokes.explanation: The visual joke of the sketch title reflecting the keyboard's damage, combined with Frank's dual justification ('I write what I know' + 'also I broke my keyboard'), is sharp. The 'I write what I know' writer's-room joke landing on Frank is perfect character integration.

jokes.text: I'm so beloved, I could do no wrong. Now, everyone's after me. UNICEF, the Gates Foundation, and what is Farmaid? Is it a drink? Is it a drug? Is it a bandage you put on a barn?
jokes.setup: Tracy reports that his morning show appearance was a disaster — but not in the way they intended.
jokes.punchline: His newfound good reputation has attracted charitable organizations. Tracy's ignorance of Farm Aid — is it a drink? a drug? a bandage for a barn? — is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Tracy's triple-hypothesis about Farm Aid — each option more absurd than the last ('a bandage you put on a barn') — is peak Tracy logic. His genuine confusion and the escalating wrongness of each guess is excellently written. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: See that's the kind of lazy standup I'll never do again!
jokes.setup: Tracy has just made a joke about Farm Aid being a bandage for a barn.
jokes.punchline: He immediately classifies his own quip as 'lazy standup' and vows to never do it again — which is itself the kind of observation a comedian makes.
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly layered meta-joke: Tracy makes an absurd observation, then meta-critiques it as 'lazy standup' — which implies Tracy has standards he's now ashamed to violate. The joke works because his self-critique is accurate (it IS the structure of lazy standup) while being delivered as earnest self-flagellation. This is the show eating itself in the best possible way.

jokes.text: 'F' you, L.L. Spells 'full'! Because you're full of B.S., Liz Lemon!
jokes.setup: Tracy is frustrated with Liz.
jokes.punchline: 'F' you, L.L.' is decoded by Tracy himself as spelling 'full' — then explained as meaning 'full of B.S.' — a baroque construction for what is essentially 'you're full of it.'
jokes.explanation: Tracy's need to explain his own insults in an overly elaborate way is deeply character-specific. The initialism logic ('F' + 'L.L.' = 'full') is Tracy's unique brand of confident wrong math. Highly quotable precisely because it's convoluted.

jokes.text: I think Bono got in my limo.
jokes.setup: Tracy is on the phone with Liz complaining about his new celebrity life.
jokes.punchline: As a throwaway conclusion, he mentions Bono has apparently gotten into his limo — treated as a minor inconvenience.
jokes.explanation: Five words, maximum impact. The economy is exceptional — Bono in the limo as an unremarkable celebrity problem, delivered as an afterthought. It's a perfect encapsulation of Tracy's new, unwanted world of do-gooders and celebrities.

jokes.text: No! And I wasn't even drinking anything. [Liz's response to 'Would you be a good mother?']
jokes.setup: Jenna asks if Liz thinks she'd be a good mother.
jokes.punchline: Liz's immediate, horrified 'No!' — and the clarification that she didn't even need liquid courage to be that harsh.
jokes.explanation: Liz's unguarded honesty is perfectly captured. The 'I wasn't even drinking anything' addendum implies that this level of bluntness normally requires alcohol — the sober 'No!' hits even harder. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: I'm in my 40s, very difficult, and not that good at playing 'la realitee.'
jokes.setup: Jenna is explaining why she needs a baby — it would excuse her from working.
jokes.punchline: Her honest self-assessment: she's 'not that good at playing la realitee' — reality spelled with a French affectation to soften the blow.
jokes.explanation: The French pronunciation of 'reality' is a perfect Jenna touch — even in self-deprecation, she's performing. The content (acknowledging she's past her prime and talentless) is painful, but the delivery mode (theatrical French) keeps it comedy rather than pathos. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Who will grow up to be a little gay fancy man.
jokes.setup: Liz says Jenna will have a child if she gets pregnant.
jokes.punchline: Jenna completes the thought — the child will grow up to be a 'little gay fancy man' — stated as fact, with no irony, just Jenna's worldview.
jokes.explanation: 'Little gay fancy man' is a specifically Jenna-flavored prediction — it's not malicious, it's just her theatrical world where this is both inevitable and somewhat aspirational. The casualness is the joke.

jokes.text: Well, good luck finding a man willing to ride that crazy train. I'll have you know, I talked with a man this morning who thinks I'd be a wonderful mother. He must be an idiot. He is an idiot.
jokes.setup: Liz doubts Jenna can find someone to have a baby with. Jenna reveals Kenneth's endorsement.
jokes.punchline: Liz calls him an idiot. Jenna agrees — 'He is an idiot' — with no defensiveness.
jokes.explanation: The rhythm of this exchange is excellent — Liz's assumption ('He must be an idiot'), Jenna's immediate agreement ('He is an idiot') without any attempt to defend Kenneth, and both of them thus united in insulting Kenneth without realizing the implication (Kenneth is the only person in the world who supports Jenna). Great two-person character comedy with a tight structure.

jokes.text: Damn it! I'm getting too old for this 'shh' sound that comes from this gas pipe.
jokes.setup: The maintenance subplot continues — the retiring worker encounters another setback.
jokes.punchline: His 'too old for this' speech is about the sound of a gas pipe — an absurdly mundane thing to be too old for, parodying the action-movie retirement trope.
jokes.explanation: The parody of the 'too old for this' action movie trope applied to a literal maintenance sound is a good sustained bit. The specific description of the 'shh' sound is funny in its precision.

jokes.text: Who are you? You're so handsome. I'm Jack Donaghy, CEO of General Electric. The question is, who are you? I'm Jack Donaghy. You were Jack Donaghy. You were magnificent.
jokes.setup: Gas-hallucinating Jack encounters what appears to be an alternate-universe version of himself.
jokes.punchline: The two Jacks meet and immediately begin one-upping each other — with the alternate Jack telling current Jack he 'was' magnificent, past tense.
jokes.explanation: Jack meeting a better version of himself is the ideal premise for his character — his competitiveness, his vanity, his identity, all compressed. The 'You were magnificent' (past tense) is the first devastating blow. Excellent character integration — only Jack's arc would produce this specific nightmare.

jokes.text: I run the General. I own an NFL team. I guest starred on Entourage. What do you do? I'll tell you what I don't do. Wear a striped tie with a striped shirt. It's called 'power clashing,' and I do it because I can.
jokes.setup: Alternate Jack lists his accomplishments to shame current Jack.
jokes.punchline: Current Jack's rebuttal is fashion: 'power clashing' — wearing stripes on stripes — which he defends as a power move.
jokes.explanation: The escalating brag list (GE, NFL team, Entourage) culminating in current Jack's pathetic counter-brag about his fashion choice is structurally excellent. 'Power clashing' as the hill Jack chooses to die on is a devastating character detail — he's reduced to defending his tie. Highly quotable. Guest star on Entourage is a perfectly calibrated celebrity lowkey-insult.

jokes.text: Wear a striped tie with a striped shirt. / It's called 'power clashing,' and I do it because I can.
jokes.setup: Real Jack criticizes Alternate Jack's outfit.
jokes.punchline: 'Power clashing' — a made-up fashion concept that Alternate Jack claims as a marker of dominance — is the perfectly absurd rebuttal.
jokes.explanation: 'Power clashing' is a genuinely funny invented concept — the confidence of the delivery ('I do it because I can') is the whole joke. Jack at his most alpha.

jokes.text: I wore this on the January cover of Meetings magazine. We made the cover during Meetings History Month? I made the cover.
jokes.setup: Jack is defending his fashion and his accomplishments.
jokes.punchline: 'Meetings magazine' — a real trade publication but ludicrously unglamorous. 'Meetings History Month' adds to the absurdity, and the alternate Jack's correction ('I made the cover') is a power move within the absurd premise.
jokes.explanation: This is excellent satire of corporate ego. Jack's proudest boast is the cover of Meetings magazine — 'Meetings History Month' is the perfectly absurd qualifying detail. The alternate Jack's correction ('I made the cover' — singular, implying current Jack was part of a group) is a precise, perfectly timed one-upmanship. Both lines work together as a sustained bit.

jokes.text: Town, Donaghy, and that's not funny. It was funny when I said it on my syndicated radio show.
jokes.setup: Jack refers to Kabletown as 'Kable Clown.' Alternate Jack corrects the name.
jokes.punchline: Alternate Jack dismisses the joke — 'that's not funny' — and claims ownership of it: he said it on his syndicated radio show (implying he's the version who thought of it first and did it better).
jokes.explanation: The idea that alternate Jack has a syndicated radio show (another accomplishment) and has already told this joke better is a sharp competitive detail. Dismissing the punchline while claiming prior ownership is a very specific power move.

jokes.text: You used to be a shark. I still am. Look at my claws! Sharks don't have claws. You don't even know what a shark is anymore!
jokes.setup: Alternate Jack says current Jack used to be a shark.
jokes.punchline: Current Jack's defense ('Look at my claws!') reveals he doesn't know sharks don't have claws. Alternate Jack's 'You don't even know what a shark is anymore!' is the devastating verdict.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes. The structure is perfect: classic metaphor ('you're a shark'), misapplication ('my claws'), factual correction, existential verdict. The comedy operates on both the literal level (claws vs. fins) and the metaphorical level (Jack has lost his predatory nature so completely he can't even conceptualize a shark correctly). Highly quotable, exceptionally structured, maximum character integration.

jokes.text: Are you building factories in Bangalore? Are you dining in the Palin White House? No. No! You're approving 'TGS' wrapped gifts, baseball caps with stupid sayings from the show written on them.
jokes.setup: Alternate Jack catalogs what current Jack should be doing vs. what he is doing.
jokes.punchline: 'The Palin White House' — a specific, pointed alternate-universe political reality embedded casually as the height of ambition.
jokes.explanation: 'Dining in the Palin White House' as the apex of Jack's alternate ambitions is both a political joke and a character joke — it's the version of success Jack would actually want, not the liberal establishment's. The contrast with 'TGS wrapped gifts' as his actual contribution is devastating.

jokes.text: What the hell is a Pwomp? It's when two fat people... I don't care!
jokes.setup: Alternate Jack sees TGS merchandise with the word 'Pwomp.'
jokes.punchline: He asks what it means, Jack begins to answer, alternate Jack cuts him off — 'I don't care!' The definition is interrupted before completion, leaving it to imagination.
jokes.explanation: The interrupted definition is funnier than any possible answer. 'It's when two fat people...' and the cutoff is a masterclass in comedic economy — the audience fills in the rest. 'I don't care!' as a punchline on top of the implied punchline is perfect structure. The word 'Pwomp' itself is funny phonetically.

jokes.text: I am a Jedi!
jokes.setup: The gas is spreading to Jack's floor. Tom, who was helping clear people out, has now also been affected.
jokes.punchline: Tom erupts with 'I am a Jedi!' — a classic gas hallucination, delivered as Tom presumably runs off.
jokes.explanation: Quick absurdist beat confirming the gas has spread. 'I am a Jedi' is a reliable pop culture hallucination joke — not particularly inventive but delivered with good economy and timing.

jokes.text: Hey, look, Tracy Jordan is ironically re-appropriating his bad past behavior as a commentary on Fitzgerald's dictum that there are no second acts in American life. I want to take a picture of him with my old-fashioned camera.
jokes.setup: Tracy is apparently doing something chaotic in public.
jokes.punchline: A bystander over-intellectualizes Tracy's behavior as Fitzgerald-level social commentary, then pivots to wanting a photo with an 'old-fashioned camera' — a hipster non-sequitur.
jokes.explanation: Sharp satire of how celebrity behavior gets over-intellectualized by cultural commentators. The Fitzgerald reference is accurate (Tracy IS failing to have a second act) while being absurdly highbrow for describing chaos. The 'old-fashioned camera' hipster pivot undercuts the intellectual posturing perfectly.

jokes.text: 'Tracy Jordan saves drowning man'? Oh, come on!
jokes.setup: Tracy keeps accidentally doing heroic things instead of embarrassing himself.
jokes.punchline: Saving a drowning man is the latest unintended act of heroism — Liz's exasperated 'Oh, come on!' says it all.
jokes.explanation: Good running escalation of Tracy's unintended good reputation. The drowning man rescue is a satisfying escalation from charity solicitation. Liz's reaction carries the joke.

jokes.text: Breathing through my mouth so I don't smell the throw-up on my shirt.
jokes.setup: Liz asks the writers what they're working on.
jokes.punchline: Lutz's contribution to the crisis: he is breathing through his mouth to avoid smelling his own shirt.
jokes.explanation: Lutz as the most pathetic writer on the staff is perfectly encapsulated here. The specificity — not just a dirty shirt, but throw-up — and his workaround are deeply character-appropriate. Good economy.

jokes.text: I would take my shirt off, but I visited my rescue chimp for his birthday last week, and another chimp got mad and bit my nipple off. He played with it, and then he kissed it, and then he ate it.
jokes.setup: Lutz is justifying why he won't remove the throw-up shirt.
jokes.punchline: The chimp ate his nipple — with a three-beat progression: played with it, kissed it, ate it.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's top jokes. The escalation structure — three beats (played, kissed, ate) — is textbook comedy craftsmanship, with each beat worse than the last. 'Kissed it' is the key middle step that makes the escalation perfect (the chimp had an emotional relationship with the nipple before consuming it). The setup (birthday visit to rescue chimp) gives it just enough mundane context to make the horror land. Lutz having a rescue chimp is itself a character joke. Close to the 'snip, snap' calibration level in terms of escalation craft.

jokes.text: Cerie, did you not bring my computer down? You said you were writing. I've only seen you use that computer to look at pictures of Nate Perkins.
jokes.setup: Liz needs her computer during the evacuation.
jokes.punchline: Cerie reveals Liz has been using the computer to look at pictures of a specific named person — presumably a crush.
jokes.explanation: Liz's secret computer use being exposed by Cerie is a good character beat. The specificity of 'Nate Perkins' (a named, presumably obscure, crush) deepens the joke beyond a generic embarrassment. Good Liz character integration.

jokes.text: Ah, pwomp!
jokes.setup: Liz is caught using her computer for non-work purposes.
jokes.punchline: She deploys the TGS slang 'pwomp' as a self-deprecating exclamation — the word whose definition was cut off in the Jack scene.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback economy — one word does the work. Liz using 'pwomp' in context tells us something about the definition (it seems to imply self-exposure/embarrassment) without completing it. The callback also confirms Liz knows the word from her show's own slang. Exceptional economy.

jokes.text: 5 years of my business life wasted, and I'm still supposed to hold your hand, your wet, yet somehow flaky hand?
jokes.setup: Jack is still angry about Liz needing his help with the 100th episode.
jokes.punchline: His complaint lands on the specific physical description of Liz's hand — 'wet, yet somehow flaky' — which is both an insult and an absurdly specific personal detail.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'wet, yet somehow flaky' is perfectly chosen — the combination of contradictory textures is grossly vivid while being a very precise Liz Lemon detail. It's both character attack and character description. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: This TV nonsense was supposed to be my stepping stone and instead it's my gravestone.
jokes.setup: Jack is processing his frustrated ambitions in front of Liz.
jokes.punchline: 'Stepping stone / gravestone' — a compact rhyming reversal that encapsulates Jack's arc.
jokes.explanation: Beautiful wordplay construction — the rhyme is not cheap because it also accurately summarizes the character's thematic arc. 'Stepping stone / gravestone' is maximally economic (six syllables, two words, complete tragic irony) and highly quotable. This is among the episode's best lines for craft, comparable to the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Sort of feel like you're going to say Leno?
jokes.setup: Jack dramatically asks 'do you know whose fault that is?' — implying a big revelation.
jokes.punchline: Liz guesses 'Leno' — a topical jab at the Jay Leno/Conan O'Brien late-night controversy — before Jack can say her name.
jokes.explanation: A topical joke that has aged somewhat (2011 reference) but lands as a character beat — Liz deflecting with a joke, guessing everything but herself. Competent misdirection.

jokes.text: Sort of feel like you're going to say Leno?
jokes.setup: Jack asks 'do you know whose fault that is?' implying he'll blame Liz.
jokes.punchline: Liz guesses Leno — at the time of airing, a timely reference to Jay Leno's controversial Tonight Show situation at NBC.
jokes.explanation: A timely NBC meta-joke — blaming Leno for everything bad at the network was in the cultural air in 2011. Works as in-universe NBC self-deprecation. Economy is good, but the joke dates itself.

jokes.text: I became the American auto industry failing to recognize that you can't fix a lemon!
jokes.setup: Jack is blaming Liz for his professional stagnation.
jokes.punchline: 'You can't fix a lemon' — simultaneously a car metaphor (lemon laws), a pun on Liz's last name, and a comment on her as a person.
jokes.explanation: This is among the episode's finest jokes. Three simultaneous meanings stack perfectly: the American auto industry metaphor (Jack as GM trying to revive a failing product), the lemon-law reference (defective car), and 'Lemon' as Liz's actual surname. The layering is seamless — it doesn't feel like a forced pun because the metaphor works independently. 'You can't fix a Lemon' is quotable, thematically resonant, and demonstrates exceptional wordplay craft. Justifies 8.7 craft score.

jokes.text: I can explain. My zipper broke.
jokes.setup: A flashback to Jack first meeting Liz. He's about to fire her.
jokes.punchline: Liz's instinctive self-defense is not about her work — it's that her zipper broke, implying she's in some state of disarray.
jokes.explanation: A quick, efficient Liz character joke — her immediate assumption is that she's being confronted about her appearance/state, not her work. 'My zipper broke' is a specific, sad detail that immediately characterizes her.

jokes.text: She hasn't got much going on. She threw a birthday party for her TV.
jokes.setup: Pete is defending Liz to Jack, saying firing her would devastate her because 'this show is her life.'
jokes.punchline: His evidence of her life's emptiness: she threw a birthday party for her TV.
jokes.explanation: 'She threw a birthday party for her TV' is a perfect Liz Lemon detail — specific, sad, extremely plausible. Pete intends it as a reason to protect her, but it functions as both a defense and a damning character portrait simultaneously. The dual reading is very well constructed.

jokes.text: If you fire Liz, then I quit. You'll never succeed by sticking your neck out for someone like her. But if that's how you feel, so be it. The important thing is that I fire someone. Pete.
jokes.setup: Pete threatens to quit if Liz is fired. Jack acknowledges his loyalty.
jokes.punchline: Jack pivots: the principle is that he must fire SOMEONE — so he fires Pete instead, with complete calm.
jokes.explanation: A masterfully structured joke. The setup-reversal is perfect: Pete's loyalty speech ('I quit if you fire Liz') backfires because Jack's principle isn't about WHO gets fired, just that someone must be. 'The important thing is that I fire someone. Pete.' is devastatingly economical. Jack's complete calm, the moral logic, and Pete's name as a two-word sentence are textbook great. This is comparable to the 8.0 anchor and surpasses it.

jokes.text: You tried to fire me? And then a week later you're like, 'Oh, I want to mentor you. Unlikely friendship.' Who do you think you are?
jokes.setup: Liz has just witnessed the flashback of Jack trying to fire her.
jokes.punchline: 'Unlikely friendship' — Liz summarizing their relationship in TV-pilot terms, naming the trope they inhabit.
jokes.explanation: Liz naming her own show's central premise as a genre trope ('unlikely friendship') is smart meta-comedy. The show is commenting on its own format from within. Liz's indignation at the late revelation is both character-specific and structurally sound.

jokes.text: I'll tell you who I was, that guy that fired Pete. And he could have run GE, but instead he got Lemoned!
jokes.setup: Jack is doubling down on blaming Liz for his career stagnation.
jokes.punchline: 'Got Lemoned' — turning Liz's surname into a verb meaning 'had your potential squandered by proximity to Liz Lemon.'
jokes.explanation: The nominalization of Liz's name into a verb — 'Lemoned' — is exceptional. It extends the lemon wordplay from joke 77 and adds another dimension: it's both a neologism and a complete character indictment. The casual confidence with which Jack deploys it suggests it should be a common word. Among the most quotable lines in the episode. Justifies 8.6 craft.

jokes.text: I knew you were supposed to push, but I didn't say anything.
jokes.setup: In the flashback moment, something was happening that Liz could have intervened in but didn't.
jokes.punchline: Liz's confession — she knew Jack was wrong/about to do something but said nothing — delivered as a matter-of-fact admission with no guilt.
jokes.explanation: A small character beat — Liz's passive complicity revealed as a gas-truth. Functional but not a standout moment.

jokes.text: I'm so glad that you're able to meet me at my break. Is this just to talk, or will you be activating my electric underwear?
jokes.setup: Jenna meets her partner Paul during a break.
jokes.punchline: Jenna's follow-up question about whether Paul will be 'activating my electric underwear' — delivered as a completely ordinary scheduling question.
jokes.explanation: 'Activating my electric underwear' asked as casually as 'are you staying for dinner' is perfect Jenna/Paul character comedy. Their relationship is built on elaborate kink normalized to mundanity — this line captures that perfectly. The specificity (electric underwear, remote activation) is exactly the right level of detail.

jokes.text: Of course not! And I'd be a terrible father. I mean, what if we had a child that was prettier than us? We'd have to leave it in a desert.
jokes.setup: Paul is asked if Jenna would be a good mother.
jokes.punchline: He agrees she'd be terrible, then escalates to desert abandonment as the logical response to a prettier-than-expected child.
jokes.explanation: The logic ('what if it was prettier than us? / We'd leave it in a desert') is beautifully inverted — the specific threat is abandonment for being too attractive, rather than too ugly. The desert detail is perfectly chosen. Paul's matter-of-fact delivery of this plan is essential to why it works. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Of course not! And I'd be a terrible father. I mean, what if we had a child that was prettier than us? We'd have to leave it in a desert.
jokes.setup: Jenna asks Paul if she'd be a good mother.
jokes.punchline: Paul's concern isn't about capability — it's about what to do with a prettier child. The solution: desert abandonment.
jokes.explanation: The logic here is demented but internally consistent with Jenna and Paul's shared vanity. Their primary parental concern is that a child might be more attractive than them. The 'leave it in a desert' solution is delivered with complete calm. This is excellent dark comedy with strong character integration — only these two would have this fear.

jokes.text: Everyone would talk about my crazy name choice. Right now it's between 'Frisbee-face,' and 'Glok-Gender-Irrelevant.'
jokes.setup: Jenna is warming to the baby idea for PR reasons.
jokes.punchline: She reveals she's already shortlisted names — 'Frisbee-face' and 'Glok-Gender-Irrelevant' — both of which are ridiculous celebrity baby names.
jokes.explanation: 'Frisbee-face' and 'Glok-Gender-Irrelevant' are both extremely well-crafted absurd celebrity baby names. 'Frisbee-face' is pure invented phonetic absurdism; 'Glok-Gender-Irrelevant' satirizes both the gender-neutral naming trend AND the hyphenated surname trend. The dash in 'Gender-Irrelevant' as a surname is a perfect specific detail.

jokes.text: I love you, Jenna Maroney. I want to hog-tie you and hide you in the luggage compartment of a Greyhound bus with just a bowl of dirty water.
jokes.setup: Paul responds to Jenna's baby name ideas with an expression of love.
jokes.punchline: His love language is kidnapping logistics — the specificity of 'Greyhound bus' and 'bowl of dirty water' as romantic provisions.
jokes.explanation: The Jenna/Paul relationship is built on theatrical dark romance, and Paul's love declaration as a kidnapping plan is perfectly calibrated for both characters. The specific details (Greyhound bus, luggage compartment, bowl of dirty water — not clean water) show craft. Jenna's accepting 'I love you too' without blinking is equally strong.

jokes.text: Kenneth Parcell may be the only man in the world who thinks you should have a child.
jokes.setup: Jenna uses Kenneth's endorsement as evidence she'd be a good mother.
jokes.punchline: Paul gently points out that Kenneth Parcell — the most credulous person alive — being your ONLY supporter is damning rather than validating.
jokes.explanation: A solid callback beat. Paul articulating what everyone already knew (Kenneth as validator is a red flag) is a clean joke with good economy.

jokes.text: Hey, Dummy! Gah, what? Whoa. You look good. You lose weight or something? Your neck, it looks looser.
jokes.setup: Denis shows up at Liz's workplace. She's surprised.
jokes.punchline: Denis's compliment: 'You look good... your neck, it looks looser.' A 'compliment' that identifies a loose neck as the attractive feature.
jokes.explanation: 'Your neck looks looser' as a compliment is a precise, gross detail that perfectly characterizes Denis's cluelessness. It implies he's studying Liz's neck specifically, which is already wrong, and his assessment is that a looser neck is an improvement. Sharp character comedy.

jokes.text: Denis, it's Dummy. I miss you, come see me. [Liz's voicemail to Denis played back]
jokes.setup: Denis claims Liz called him. Liz denies it.
jokes.punchline: The voicemail plays — Liz did call, identifying herself as 'Dummy' and admitting she misses him.
jokes.explanation: The gas-induced voicemail catch is well structured — Liz's denial followed by audio evidence. 'It's Dummy' as her self-identification on a voicemail is both sad and funny. The message is perfect in its simplicity.

jokes.text: Things were better 5 years ago, Jack. I was in my 30s and everything!
jokes.setup: Liz is nostalgic under the gas's influence.
jokes.punchline: 'I was in my 30s and everything!' — 'and everything' as a trailing addendum implying the 30s were a comprehensive golden era.
jokes.explanation: 'And everything' as a vague addendum to being in her 30s is a specific kind of Liz Lemon nostalgia — the decade itself was the achievement. The line is economically delivered and highly quotable.

jokes.text: Things were better 5 years ago, Jack. I was in my 30s and everything!
jokes.setup: Liz is nostalgic for her simpler pre-Jack life.
jokes.punchline: 'I was in my 30s and everything!' — 'and everything' doing significant work here as a wistful acknowledgment that being in her 30s was the primary perk of 5 years ago.
jokes.explanation: 'And everything' is perfect. It implies that simply being in your 30s was the key advantage, and everything else followed. The bathos of age as the primary nostalgic asset is very Liz. Well-calibrated economy.

jokes.text: Waaaz aaap! [from Denis's voicemail greeting, in the style of the Budweiser 'Wassup' commercial]
jokes.setup: The voicemail greeting plays before Liz's embarrassing message.
jokes.punchline: Denis's voicemail is a 'Wassup' impression — revealing his personality as someone who would still be doing that bit years later.
jokes.explanation: The dated Budweiser reference is appropriate character comedy for Denis — he's exactly the type. Functions as character shorthand but isn't particularly inventive beyond the identification.

jokes.text: 'cause down deep, you still got all kinds of queer feelings for me. That's why I knew some day you'd be all vulnerable from a gas leak or a coma or a super period.
jokes.setup: Denis insists Liz still has feelings for him.
jokes.punchline: His theory: she'd become vulnerable via 'gas leak or a coma or a super period' — the escalating series of vulnerability inducers is absurd.
jokes.explanation: 'Super period' as the third option after 'gas leak' and 'coma' is perfect escalation. The word 'super' applied to a period is an inspired comic choice — it's exactly Denis's vocabulary. He's been planning for all these scenarios, which is both pathetic and deeply weird. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: I'm a Duffy, Liz. And us Duffys, we didn't give up when we got kicked out of Ireland. We didn't give up when America sent us back. And we didn't give up when Ireland then just set us adrift on a log, all right?
jokes.setup: Denis refuses to give up on winning Liz back.
jokes.punchline: The Duffy family history escalates through three increasingly catastrophic rejections — kicked out of Ireland, sent back by America, then set adrift on a log — as a source of pride.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's top jokes. The three-beat escalation is textbook excellent: kicked out of Ireland (plausible Irish-American backstory), sent back by America (escalation — even America rejected them), set adrift on a log by Ireland (peak absurdism — Ireland took them back only to float them away). The logic follows perfectly and gets worse each time. 'All right?' as the trailing close is perfectly Denis. The structure rivals the 'snip, snap' calibration for escalation craft. Highly quotable and completely character-specific.

tmdb_overview: With their show targeted for cancellation, the "TGS" crew desperately scramble to mount a top-notch production for their 100th episode. Meanwhile, Jack reconsiders a vital decision in his life, and Jenna mulls over motherhood.
insight: Absurdist escalation drives 67 jokes across 38 minutes, hitting 77.2 despite low single-joke impact.
